subject: Cross-layer feature reuse patterns and their implications for structured pruning in vision-language models

Topic: Cross-layer feature reuse patterns and their implications for structured pruning in vision-language models

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-346)
response:
Cross-layer feature reuse in vision-language models refers to the empirical phenomenon where intermediate representations — attention heads, MLP activations, or entire residual stream slices — encode semantically similar information across non-adjacent layers, often with measurable cosine similarity above 0.9 between layers that are 6–12 steps apart. The central question is whether this redundancy is exploitable: if layers are doing nearly the same work, can you remove or merge them without degrading task performance, and does the answer differ between the vision encoder, the language decoder, and the cross-modal alignment components? Structured pruning — removing entire heads, layers, or channels rather than individual weights — is attractive because it yields actual inference speedups on real hardware, unlike sparse unstructured pruning which requires specialized kernels to benefit from. The key concepts to hold together are: layer similarity metrics (CKA, representational similarity analysis), the distinction between redundancy and robustness (a layer may look redundant until you remove it and discover it was absorbing gradient noise), and the architectural asymmetry between vision and language towers in models like LLaVA or Flamingo.

What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is task-conditional redundancy: a layer that appears redundant on a standard similarity metric computed over held-out ImageNet captions may be load-bearing for rare but critical operations — fine-grained spatial grounding, negation handling, or out-of-distribution compositional queries — that simply don't surface in aggregate statistics. Pruning decisions made on bulk similarity measures are implicitly making a bet about which capabilities the deployment distribution actually needs, and that bet is almost never made explicit.

When you measure cross-layer similarity in a vision-language model, what specifically are you comparing — the weight matrices, the activations over a dataset, or something else — and why does that choice determine whether your redundancy estimate is meaningful?

response:
The choice of what to compare is not cosmetic — it determines whether you're measuring structural redundancy (what the model could compute) or functional redundancy (what it actually computes on your data). Comparing weight matrices directly, as in early work on BERT layer similarity, uses metrics like CKA on the parameter tensors themselves, but this is largely meaningless for vision-language models because the same weight matrix applied to different input distributions (a visual token vs. a language token) produces functionally different transformations. The dominant and more defensible approach is activation-based comparison: you run a representative dataset through the model and compute CKA or representational similarity between the activation matrices at layers i and j, where each row is one token's hidden state. Raghu et al.'s SVCCA work and subsequent CKA papers (Kornblith et al., 2019) showed that activation-based similarity is invariant to orthogonal transformations of the representation space, which matters because two layers can have very different weights but produce geometrically equivalent representations up to rotation. In models like LLaVA-1.5, empirical probing work has found that vision encoder layers 16–24 (of 24 in CLIP ViT-L) show pairwise CKA above 0.85 on COCO-style data, suggesting high redundancy — but this similarity collapses toward 0.4–0.5 when you switch the dataset to spatially demanding tasks like RefCOCO, revealing that the estimate was dataset-conditional all along. A third option, less common but arguably sharpest, is to compare functional behavior via interchange interventions: you patch the activation from layer i into the position of layer j and measure downstream task degradation, which directly tests substitutability rather than geometric similarity. The choice matters because CKA can tell you two layers are similar while interchange intervention reveals they are not substitutable — and only the latter predicts whether pruning will hurt.

The calibration dataset needs to satisfy at least three properties to produce generalizable pruning decisions: sufficient modal coverage (images that stress the vision encoder's spatial, semantic, and compositional axes simultaneously), linguistic diversity in the paired queries (not just captions but questions requiring negation, counting, and spatial reasoning), and tail-task representation, meaning rare but load-bearing operations must appear with enough frequency to influence the similarity estimates. The practical failure mode is that most pruning papers calibrate on COCO or CC3M subsets, which are caption-dominated and spatially undemanding — Fang et al.'s work on EVA-CLIP pruning and the ShortGPT experiments on LLaMA-based VLMs both used calibration sets under 512 samples drawn from caption distributions, which systematically overestimates redundancy in layers responsible for fine-grained grounding. A useful analogy from the quantization literature is instructive: GPTQ and AWQ both showed that calibration set size matters less than calibration set diversity, with 128 carefully chosen samples outperforming 2048 homogeneous ones — the same logic almost certainly applies to pruning, but has not been rigorously tested in the VLM setting. The interaction with unknown deployment distributions is where the problem becomes structurally hard: you are essentially trying to estimate a property (layer substitutability) that is a function of the deployment distribution, without access to that distribution, and the error is asymmetric — over-pruning a layer that turns out to be load-bearing for your actual users is not recoverable without retraining. One partial mitigation is to use a worst-case rather than average-case similarity criterion: instead of pruning layers whose mean pairwise CKA exceeds a threshold, prune only layers that exceed the threshold across a battery of maximally diverse tasks, which is the implicit logic behind benchmarks like MMMU and SeedBench being used as pruning validators in recent work from groups at Microsoft Research and Tsinghua. The deeper tension is that this conservative strategy requires knowing what "maximally diverse" means before deployment, which partially reintroduces the unknown-distribution problem in a different form — you've traded one unknown (deployment data) for another (the space of possible tasks), and no current pruning framework makes this tradeoff explicit.

Given that pruning decisions are made once but deployed across a shifting distribution, is there a principled argument for making pruning itself adaptive at inference time — and what architectural or computational constraints make that either feasible or self-defeating?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-349)
response:
The principled argument for inference-time adaptive pruning exists and draws from two converging lines of work: mixture-of-experts routing, where a learned gating function dynamically activates a subset of parameters per token, and early-exit networks, where a confidence signal determines how many layers a given input traverses. In both cases the argument is the same — input complexity is heterogeneous, so fixed compute allocation is structurally wasteful, and a spatial grounding query should route through different layers than a simple object-naming query even within the same deployed model. The most concrete recent instantiation is in models like Mixture-of-Depths (Raposo et al., 2024) and layer-skipping work on LLaMA variants, where tokens dynamically bypass layers based on a lightweight router, achieving roughly 20–30% FLOPs reduction with under 2% degradation on standard benchmarks — but critically, these results are on language-only models, and the vision-language transfer is not established. The architectural constraint that makes this hard in VLMs specifically is the cross-modal attention bottleneck: in models like Flamingo or LLaVA, there are layers whose job is to align visual and linguistic representations, and these layers cannot be safely skipped for visually-grounded queries without breaking the semantic binding that downstream layers depend on — the router has no cheap way to know in advance whether a query will need that binding. The computational constraint is more subtle: the router itself must be fast enough that its overhead doesn't eat the savings from skipping, which is manageable for layer-level routing but becomes problematic if you need per-head or per-channel decisions, where the routing computation can approach the cost of just running the head. The self-defeating failure mode appears when adaptive pruning is applied to a model that was not trained with routing in mind — post-hoc layer skipping without router fine-tuning produces inconsistent residual stream states that later layers were never trained to handle, which is why ShortGPT-style layer dropping shows sharper degradation curves than MoD-style trained routing despite similar nominal sparsity levels.

The asymmetry is empirically well-supported: vision encoders in CLIP-based VLMs tolerate significantly higher layer removal rates than the language decoder before task performance degrades, with several pruning studies finding that removing 30–40% of ViT-L layers produces under 3% drop on VQAv2, while removing an equivalent fraction of the LLM decoder layers produces 8–15% drop on the same benchmark. One clean demonstration comes from the LLaVA-Prune line of work, where pruning the CLIP vision tower aggressively (down to 16 of 24 layers) while preserving the Vicuna decoder nearly intact produced competitive results on caption and VQA tasks, but the same compression ratio applied decoder-side caused catastrophic degradation on tasks requiring multi-step reasoning — suggesting the decoder is the computational bottleneck for reasoning while the vision tower is over-provisioned for most standard tasks. The task-dependence of this asymmetry is where it gets precise: for retrieval tasks like image-text matching, the vision tower's later layers are critical because they produce the embedding that gets compared, so pruning tolerance inverts — you can remove more decoder layers than encoder layers without hurting recall@5 on MSCOCO retrieval. For grounding tasks like RefCOCO, both towers become load-bearing simultaneously but in different ways: the vision encoder's mid-to-late layers (roughly layers 12–20 in ViT-L) encode spatial position information that grounding depends on, while the decoder's early-to-mid layers handle the linguistic parsing of the referring expression, and pruning either set selectively degrades only the corresponding failure mode. Generation tasks show yet another pattern: perplexity and fluency are almost entirely decoder-determined, so the vision tower can be pruned heavily without affecting output coherence as long as the cross-modal projection layer is preserved, which explains why generation-focused VLM compression papers consistently report more aggressive vision-side pruning ratios. The practical implication that most compression papers ignore is that a single pruning configuration cannot be Pareto-optimal across retrieval, generation, and grounding simultaneously — the optimal pruning mask is task-family-specific, and deploying one compressed model for all three use cases means accepting suboptimality on at least two.

The claim that the projection layer is universally the most compression-sensitive component is approximately but not exactly right — it is the most brittle component, which is a distinct property. Sensitivity means performance degrades smoothly with compression; brittleness means performance holds until a threshold and then collapses discontinuously, which is what empirical work on LLaVA's MLP projection consistently shows: you can quantize it to 8-bit with negligible loss, to 4-bit with moderate loss, but at 3-bit or below, cross-modal grounding collapses faster than either tower does at equivalent bit-widths, suggesting the projection is operating near its information-theoretic capacity even at full precision. Structurally, the projection layer in LLaVA-style models is a 2-layer MLP mapping from CLIP's 1024-dimensional output to the LLM's embedding dimension (e.g., 4096 for Vicuna-13B), and its job is not just dimensionality matching but learned re-encoding — it must translate visual features organized around contrastive image-text alignment into a token space organized around next-token prediction, two objectives that are not naturally aligned. When you apply structured pruning directly to this MLP — removing neurons from the hidden layer — you are compressing the only site where this representational translation occurs, and unlike pruning a redundant transformer layer, there is no parallel pathway or residual connection that can compensate; the information simply does not reach the decoder. The most concrete failure signature is modality collapse under projection pruning: the decoder begins treating visual tokens as uninformative and reverts to language-prior-dominated generation, producing fluent but visually ungrounded text — this is measurable as a sharp drop in CHAIR hallucination metrics and a simultaneous increase in BLEU on caption tasks, because the model is generating plausible captions from language statistics alone. Recent work on Q-Former architectures (BLIP-2) suggests one structural mitigation: cross-attention-based projection distributes the translation function across multiple layers and heads, making it more gracefully compressible than a single MLP bottleneck, with InstructBLIP showing roughly 40% Q-Former parameter reduction at under 2% VQA degradation — but this comes at the cost of increased inference latency from the added cross-attention operations.

The distinction between genuine repair and decoder compensation is not academic — it determines whether your pruned-then-finetuned model is robust to distribution shift or merely overfit to the finetuning task's statistical regularities. Genuine repair would manifest as restored mutual information between visual token representations and ground-truth scene properties, measurable via probing classifiers trained on the projection output: if post-finetuning probes recover spatial position, object identity, and attribute binding at rates comparable to the unpruned model, the translation function is restored. Decoder compensation would manifest differently: probe accuracy on projection outputs remains degraded, but the decoder develops stronger attention to whatever residual visual signal survives, potentially combined with heavier reliance on linguistic co-occurrence statistics — you would see this as asymmetric attention weight concentration on visual tokens in early decoder layers post-finetuning, accompanied by increased sensitivity to language-prior perturbations like shuffled captions. The empirical signature that most cleanly separates the two is performance on novel visual concepts absent from the finetuning distribution: a decoder compensating via language statistics will fail on out-of-vocabulary visual categories or unusual spatial configurations because it has no linguistic prior to fall back on, while genuine projection repair would generalize because the translation function itself is restored. Concrete evidence that compensation dominates comes from LLaVA ablations where post-pruning finetuning recovers VQAv2 accuracy to within 1–2% of baseline but CHAIR hallucination scores remain 15–25% worse than baseline, indicating the model is generating plausible text without genuine visual grounding — a classic compensation signature. The methodologically cleanest distinguishing experiment would be a vision-scrambling probe: finetune on normal data, then at inference time replace visual tokens with tokens from a different image while keeping the text query constant, and measure whether the model's output changes appropriately; a genuinely repaired projection should produce outputs that track the new image, while a compensating decoder will produce outputs that track the text query regardless of visual input.

The implication is partially supported but breaks down at a critical boundary: larger decoders do appear to compensate more effectively for degraded visual input on language-proximal tasks, which is why LLaVA-1.5 with a 13B decoder recovers from aggressive vision-tower pruning better than the 7B variant on VQAv2 and GQA, but this advantage essentially vanishes on tasks requiring precise spatial reasoning or pixel-level grounding where there is no linguistic prior strong enough to substitute. The scaling evidence is most clearly visible in the InternVL and LLaVA-NeXT family: as decoder size increases from 7B to 34B, performance on caption and commonsense visual QA tasks becomes increasingly decoupled from vision encoder quality, with some 34B models achieving competitive MMBench scores even with CLIP encoders frozen at reduced resolution — but the same models show no such robustness improvement on spatial tasks like CVBench or What'sUp, where encoder quality remains the binding constraint regardless of decoder size. This suggests a task-conditional scaling law: the marginal return on decoder parameters for visually-grounded tasks diminishes faster than for language-proximal tasks, and there exists a decoder size beyond which additional parameters primarily improve linguistic coherence rather than visual understanding. The architectural allocation prediction that follows is counterintuitive: future VLMs optimized for grounding should not follow the current trend of pairing a frozen medium-sized vision encoder with an ever-larger decoder, but should instead allocate more parameters to the vision side or the projection interface — which is precisely the design logic behind models like InternViT-6B and the Cambrian-1 spatial vision aggregator, both of which invest heavily in vision-side capacity rather than defaulting to decoder scaling. The strongest version of this prediction is that the current CLIP ViT-L plus large-LLM paradigm is architecturally mismatched for grounding-heavy deployments: CLIP was trained on image-text contrastive objectives that discard spatial detail in favor of global semantics, so no amount of decoder scaling can recover spatial information that was never encoded. What this predicts practically is a bifurcation in VLM architecture: caption-and-reasoning models will continue scaling decoders with cheap vision encoders, while grounding-and-localization models will require fundamentally different encoder architectures, possibly trained on dense prediction objectives rather than contrastive ones.
